Statements from the client or witnesses

notes: Let’s take a look at a practical tool that helps you gather and organize all the important details — the MVA (Motor Vehicle Accident) or MVC (Motor Vehicle Collision) Questionnaire. This document isn’t the actual client questionnaire but rather a reference sheet — a summarized version of the key information you’ll need when handling a case. Think of it as your cheat sheet during the opening of a claim. * Purpose of the MVA Questionnaire * This form serves as your roadmap. It helps you: ⦁ Keep all accident-related details organized in one place — from basic client information to vehicle and insurance details. ⦁ Avoid missing any critical information during calls or documentation. ⦁ Quickly access verified details when speaking with adjusters or drafting letters of representation. But most importantly, it helps ensure confidentiality — that you only share information you’re authorized to provide. Before calling the insurance adjuster or any third party, always review this sheet first. This ensures you: ⦁ Have all the necessary case information ready. ⦁ Stay focused during the call, even when the conversation gets engaging. ⦁ Avoid accidentally sharing restricted details such as index information or any data that could allow the other party (especially the at-fault insurance company) to contact the client directly. Remember — sharing those kinds of details could lead to backdoor negotiations that might undermine the client’s settlement and even risk the firm losing the client. Key Sections: 🔹 Client and Insurance Information - Lists both 1st Party (our client’s insurance) and 3rd Party (at-fault driver’s insurance). Always double-check accuracy — even a small error in a policy or claim number can delay processing. 🔹 Accident Details (Facts of Loss) - Covers when, where, and how the accident happened — this must align with the details reported in the claim and what we refer to as the “Facts of Loss.” 🔹 Police Report and Witnesses - Indicates whether there’s a police report, the responding department, and any witnesses. These support the client’s version of events later on. 🔹 Injuries and Medical Treatment - Outlines what injuries were sustained, whether the client was transported by ambulance, and where they are currently treating. This section connects the medical aspect of the case to the liability. 🔹 Vehicle Information - Lists both the client’s and the defendant’s vehicle details — make, model, and condition (drivable or not). It also notes visible damages for documentation consistency. Key Takeaway: - The MVA Questionnaire isn’t just a form — it’s a protection tool for both the client and the firm. - It helps you open claims efficiently, stay organized, and safeguard sensitive information while maintaining professionalism and accuracy throughout the process.

boxes: In most cases, Attorneys will direct you to open the PIP (Personal Injury Protection) and/or UM (Uninsured/Underinsured Motorist) claims immediately after intake. These coverages are often available through the client's own insurance and can help with early medical treatment or when the at-fault party is uninsured or underinsured.

However, it's important to note that some law firms prioritize opening the Bodily Injury (BI) claim first, especially when liability is clear and prompt communication with the at-fault party’s insurer is necessary.
As a Claims Specialist, always follow firm-specific protocols and Attorney instructions regarding the order in which claims are opened.

It’s better to clarify than to assume.”

boxes: If the claim is not opened during the initial call, set a follow-up reminder within 24–48 hours to confirm status and ensure progress.
Always confirm and double check the obtained claim number, name of adjuster (spelling), adjuster’s phone number, adjuster’s fax number and adjuster’s preferred mode of communication.
NEVER provide the personal information of the client when opening a Third party claim (BI). Only provide the vehicle information (make and model) if asked.

notes: 📊 Policy Limits Overview: Policy Limits define the maximum payout an insurer will provide under a specific coverage type. Tip: Always clarify the type of limit when discussing coverage with insurance adjusters to ensure you understand how the policy will respond to claims.

notes: "A Dropped Case is one that fails to progress towards resolution, often due to reasons like client withdrawal, lack of evidence, or failure to meet deadlines. It is crucial that such cases are handled with care and documented properly to ensure firm integrity and compliance. Document the reason for the case discontinuation, and ensure that any necessary closing actions are taken. This will protect the firm in the event of later inquiries. Maintain open communication with the client throughout the process. If they are considering dropping the case, make sure they understand the full impact of that decision. Always ensure the case is officially closed in the system once the client or other circumstances have led to the case's dismissal, and take any necessary steps to ensure compliance with the law and insurance policies."

notes: "A Dropped Case can happen for several reasons, each of which must be carefully documented and managed. Let’s go over some of the common reasons a case might be discontinued: Client unresponsiveness or withdrawal—if a client decides to stop cooperating or pulls out of the case entirely. Liability issues—if we cannot establish fault or liability with sufficient evidence. Coverage problems—either the insurance company denies the claim or the policy limits are insufficient to cover the damages. Client treatment non-compliance—if the client fails to complete medical treatments, it can undermine the credibility and validity of their claim. Discovery of conflicting or fraudulent information—this may force us to drop the case to avoid legal repercussions. Proper handling and documentation of these situations are vital to maintaining integrity in the claims process."
